The Institute of Advanced Study at Central European University (IAS CEU) is inviting applications for its 2027/28 Global Invisible University Fellowship Program, offering an exceptional opportunity for scholars, researchers, writers and visual artists to pursue independent work within an international and interdisciplinary academic community.

Hosted primarily in Budapest, Hungary, the IAS CEU fellowship programme brings together highly accomplished senior academics, promising early-career scholars, threatened scholars, writers and visual artists whose work connects with some of the most pressing intellectual, political, social, environmental and institutional challenges facing societies today.

For the 2027/28 academic year, the Institute is offering several fellowship pathways, including the Junior and Senior Residential Fellowship, Artist in Residence Fellowship, Residential and Non-residential Fellowships for Threatened Scholars, and Residential Affiliated Fellowships.

Depending on the fellowship, successful applicants may spend between three and nine months at IAS CEU, while non-residential opportunities for threatened scholars can extend from six to 12 months.

The fellowships form an important part of the Global Invisible University (GIU), a wider CEU initiative that integrates research, teaching, mentoring and civic engagement while seeking new ways of responding to challenges affecting universities, scholars and access to knowledge around the world.

About the IAS CEU Global Invisible University Fellowship Program

The Institute of Advanced Study at CEU provides an intellectual environment in which fellows can concentrate on their individual research and creative projects while participating in a broader interdisciplinary community.

IAS CEU is seeking scholars who are interested not only in advancing their own research but also in contributing to conversations about new approaches to producing, sharing and transferring knowledge.

The fellowship programme is envisioned as the principal research arm of the Global Invisible University.

The initiative draws on approximately 15 years of institutional experience and practices developed by IAS CEU and combines this established research infrastructure with GIU’s broader ambition to rethink higher education in response to contemporary global challenges.

These include challenges arising from:

  • War and armed conflict;
  • Forced displacement;
  • Autocratization and democratic decline;
  • Restrictions on academic freedom;
  • Political repression;
  • Commercial pressures affecting higher education;
  • Inequalities in the production and accessibility of knowledge;
  • Threats faced by scholars and academic institutions; and
  • Wider transformations affecting universities and research communities globally.

Through this programme, CEU aims to bring together researchers and creative practitioners who can contribute to an international academic environment centred on rigorous research, interdisciplinary exchange and new approaches to knowledge production.

What Is the Global Invisible University?

The Global Invisible University (GIU) is a strategic initiative intended to develop a new model of a “university for the future.”

Rather than approaching research, teaching and public engagement as entirely separate activities, GIU seeks to integrate them.

The programme combines university-level education, mentoring and research involving students and scholars, including academics affected by authoritarianism, war, displacement and other crises that constrain academic life.

The wider objective is to contribute to more resilient, democratic and open societies and academic institutions.

The 2027/28 IAS CEU fellowships therefore offer more than simply time away from normal professional responsibilities. Fellows are expected to become members of an experimental academic community in which independent research, intellectual collaboration and discussions about the future of knowledge and higher education can reinforce one another.

IAS CEU Fellowship Duration for 2027/28

Residential fellowships are available for different periods, allowing fellows to participate for between three and nine months depending on the fellowship type and approved arrangement.

Potential residential periods include:

  1. Nine-month fellowship: October 2027 to June 2028.
  2. Three-month short fall semester: October to December 2027.
  3. Five-month fall semester: October 2027 to February 2028.
  4. Six-month spring semester: January to June 2028.

Separate arrangements apply to some fellowship categories, particularly the Artist in Residence and Threatened Scholars programmes.

Applicants should therefore carefully review the individual call corresponding to the fellowship for which they intend to apply.

Types of IAS CEU Fellowships Available for 2027/28

There are several fellowship pathways within the IAS CEU programme. Candidates should select the opportunity that most closely corresponds to their academic background, professional situation and proposed project.

1. Junior and Senior Residential Fellowship

The Junior and Senior Residential Fellowship, also described as the core fellowship programme, is designed for scholars who want to spend between three and nine months in Budapest pursuing their own research.

Both junior and senior scholars are considered within this programme.

Core fellows are given an opportunity to work on their research while becoming part of the interdisciplinary intellectual community at IAS CEU.

Importantly, Junior and Senior Core Fellows receive:

  • A fellowship stipend;
  • Accommodation at the Raoul Wallenberg Guesthouse;
  • An opportunity to pursue their own independent research;
  • Access to the IAS CEU intellectual community;
  • Research support and institutional resources; and
  • Opportunities for interdisciplinary exchange with other fellows and the wider CEU community.

Applicants should consult the dedicated Residential Core Fellowship call for the detailed eligibility criteria, financial terms and application requirements.

2. Artist in Residence Fellowship

IAS CEU also recognises creative practice as an important component of intellectual and societal engagement.

For 2027/28, the Institute offers two Artist in Residence opportunities:

  • One Writer in Residence Fellowship
  • One Visual Artist in Residence Fellowship

These fellowships are offered competitively to writers and visual artists whose work engages with the objectives of the Global Invisible University in innovative and convincing ways.

Eligible areas of creative practice may include, among others:

  • Poetry;
  • Prose;
  • Drama;
  • Screenwriting;
  • Playwriting;
  • Film;
  • Digital applications; and
  • Other forms of visual media.

Artist in Residence fellowships may last for up to five months, with a minimum residence period of three months.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate how their creative work connects meaningfully with the broader intellectual and societal aims of GIU.

3. Residential and Non-residential Fellowships for Threatened Scholars

An especially important component of the programme is dedicated to scholars facing serious threats to their ability to work, research or participate freely in academic life.

The Fellowships for Threatened Scholars are intended for scholars at risk because of circumstances including:

  • Loss of employment;
  • Harassment;
  • Violence;
  • Legal persecution;
  • Political or civic positions of dissent;
  • Identity;
  • Critical scholarship;
  • Exercise of academic freedom; or
  • Immediate exposure to active military conflict.

The programme therefore recognises that academic freedom and the ability to conduct research cannot be taken for granted in many parts of the world.

Scholars living in or coming from areas affected by active military conflict may also qualify where the conflict directly affects them.

In addition to residential opportunities, IAS CEU provides non-residential fellowships exclusively for Threatened Scholars.

These non-residential fellowships are available for periods ranging from six to 12 months, during the period from August 2027 to July 2028.

Candidates interested in this pathway should carefully consult the specific Threatened Scholars fellowship call because eligibility is linked to the applicant’s circumstances as well as their scholarly work.

4. Residential Affiliated Fellowships

IAS CEU also welcomes a limited number of Affiliated Fellows each year.

These opportunities differ significantly from the funded core fellowships.

Affiliated Fellows typically have their own external fellowship or other funding and use that support to spend all or part of their research period at IAS CEU.

The minimum stay for an affiliated fellowship is three months.

Prospective applicants should note that:

  • Affiliated Fellows do not receive a stipend from IAS CEU;
  • Housing may or may not be provided by the Institute;
  • Applicants typically rely on external fellowship funding or another independent source of financial support; and
  • The fellowship allows researchers to become part of the IAS CEU academic environment during their research period.

Applicants requiring full financial support should therefore pay close attention to the differences between the Affiliated Fellowship and the funded fellowship categories.

Research Areas for the Global Invisible University Fellowships

A major component of the selection process is the relationship between an applicant’s proposed project and the intellectual priorities of the Global Invisible University.

Applicants are expected to connect their research or proposed work with at least one of eight key GIU thematic areas.

1. Democratization, De-democratization and Re-democratization

This thematic area addresses processes through which democratic systems emerge, weaken, transform or recover.

Projects may explore questions surrounding democratic institutions, political participation, authoritarian tendencies, democratic resilience and transitions between different political systems.

2. Politics of History, Memory and Culture Wars

This area encompasses the political use and interpretation of history and collective memory, as well as contemporary cultural conflicts.

Relevant work may examine:

  • Historical narratives;
  • Collective memory;
  • Culture wars;
  • Nationalist discourse;
  • Transnationalist discourse; and
  • The relationship between identity, politics, culture and interpretations of the past.

3. Political Economy and Global Inequalities

Researchers working on political economy, economic structures, inequality and related global challenges may find this thematic area particularly relevant.

Projects could address the relationships between political institutions, economic systems, distribution of resources and inequalities within or between societies.

4. Human Rights and Justice

This research priority focuses on human rights and justice in the context of international and comparative law.

Researchers may investigate legal institutions, rights protection, comparative legal systems, international law and broader questions surrounding justice and accountability.

5. Crisis of Multilateralism and Global Institutions

This area examines the changing role and effectiveness of international and regional institutions and alliances.

Potential research subjects may include:

  • Multilateral organisations;
  • International cooperation;
  • Regional institutions;
  • Global institutions;
  • Political alliances;
  • International governance; and
  • Contemporary challenges facing multilateralism.

6. Politics of the Anthropocene, Climate Justice and Natural Resources

Environmental and climate-related research is another important GIU priority.

Relevant research may explore:

  • The politics of the Anthropocene;
  • Climate justice;
  • Environmental governance;
  • Natural resources;
  • Political and social responses to climate change; and
  • Inequalities associated with environmental change and resource distribution.

7. Old and New Media and Their Networks

This theme examines both established and emerging media environments and the networks through which information is created, circulated and contested.

Topics may include:

  • Information warfare;
  • Media networks;
  • Digital communication;
  • Safer use of media and digital systems;
  • Securitization; and
  • Transformations in information ecosystems.

8. Epistemological Problems of Social Sciences in the Digital Age

The eighth thematic area addresses fundamental questions about how knowledge and evidence are created and evaluated in an increasingly digital environment.

The programme specifically identifies areas such as:

  • Evidentiary procedures;
  • Truth claims;
  • Archival practices;
  • Digital transformations of research;
  • Epistemological challenges in the social sciences; and
  • “Forensic social sciences.”

Applicants do not necessarily need to address all eight areas. However, their proposed work is expected to demonstrate a meaningful relationship with at least one of these priorities.

Who Is IAS CEU Looking For?

IAS CEU describes its residential fellowships as opportunities for both highly accomplished senior scholars and promising younger scholars.

The programme is particularly relevant to individuals who want concentrated time to advance an independent research project while also participating in an interdisciplinary academic environment.

Depending on the specific fellowship, IAS CEU is seeking:

  • Junior scholars;
  • Senior and established scholars;
  • Researchers in the social sciences;
  • Researchers in the humanities;
  • Scholars whose research addresses GIU thematic priorities;
  • Writers;
  • Visual artists;
  • Scholars facing threats to their academic freedom or personal safety;
  • Scholars affected by active military conflict; and
  • Externally funded scholars interested in becoming Affiliated Fellows.

Applicants should not assume that general alignment with social sciences or humanities is sufficient. The proposed project should also demonstrate clear relevance to the broader goals and thematic priorities of the Global Invisible University.

Selection Process for the IAS CEU Fellowships

Applicants should be aware that admission to the IAS CEU fellowship programme is highly competitive.

Applications undergo a rigorous peer-review process, with the final decision made by an independent Selection Committee.

According to IAS CEU, major considerations include:

  1. Excellence of the proposed research

    The intellectual strength and overall quality of the research proposal are central to the assessment.

  2. Applicant’s track record

    The Selection Committee considers the applicant’s previous scholarly or professional accomplishments.

  3. Thematic relevance

    Proposed research must demonstrate relevance to the broader objectives and research priorities of the Global Invisible University.

Because the fellowships are highly competitive, applicants should ensure that their proposals clearly communicate the importance, originality and feasibility of their proposed work rather than relying solely on academic credentials.

Why Budapest Is Important to the Fellowship Experience

Although Central European University’s main campus is located in Vienna, Austria, CEU maintains a significant research presence in Budapest, Hungary.

Several CEU research institutes, centres and resources operate in Budapest, including:

  • The Institute of Advanced Study;
  • CEU Democracy Institute;
  • Blinken OSA Archivum;
  • Center for Ethics and Law in Biomedicine;
  • Artistic and cultural programmes;
  • Non-degree educational programmes; and
  • The Budapest branch of the CEU Library.

The fellowship programme is therefore situated within a broader intellectual ecosystem rather than functioning as an isolated research residency.

IAS CEU also views Budapest as an important environment for thinking about political and social transformation, including processes of re-democratization.

The programme aims to encourage new relationships and synergies not only among IAS fellows but also between fellows and educational and civil society organisations in Hungary and the broader region.

Benefits of Joining the IAS CEU Intellectual Community

While exact financial benefits depend on the fellowship category, participation in IAS CEU offers fellows an opportunity to become part of a multidisciplinary and international research environment.

Potential advantages include:

  • Dedicated time to pursue independent research or creative work;
  • Participation in an interdisciplinary community;
  • Interaction with scholars working across social sciences and humanities;
  • Engagement with CEU institutes, research centres and intellectual networks;
  • Opportunities for scholarly exchange and collaboration;
  • Access to research support infrastructure;
  • Participation in conversations around research, teaching and civic engagement;
  • An opportunity to explore new approaches to knowledge production and transfer; and
  • Residence in Budapest for eligible residential fellows.

For Junior and Senior Core Fellows specifically, IAS CEU states that fellows receive a stipend and accommodation at the Raoul Wallenberg Guesthouse.

Benefits and financial conditions vary across fellowship categories, so candidates should review the individual call before applying.

Application Deadline for IAS CEU Fellowships 2027/28

Application deadlines vary according to the individual IAS CEU fellowship call.

The general programme information provided by IAS CEU directs applicants to its dedicated fellowship and open-call pages for the applicable application deadlines and detailed instructions.

Applicants should therefore check the official IAS CEU Open Calls page and the individual fellowship call before submitting an application, rather than assuming that all 2027/28 fellowships share one closing date.

Because individual fellowship programmes may have different requirements, funding arrangements and deadlines, prospective applicants should begin reviewing the appropriate call as early as possible.

How to Apply for IAS CEU Fellowships 2027/28

Candidates should apply through the official Institute of Advanced Study at Central European University fellowship portal and relevant fellowship call.

Official fellowship information and open calls are available through:

IAS CEU Fellowships:
https://ias.ceu.edu/fellowships-ias-ceu

Applicants should first identify which fellowship best matches their circumstances:

  • Junior or Senior Residential Fellowship;
  • Writer in Residence Fellowship;
  • Visual Artist in Residence Fellowship;
  • Residential or Non-residential Fellowship for Threatened Scholars; or
  • Residential Affiliated Fellowship.

They should then open the corresponding official call and carefully review its eligibility requirements, application documents, financial conditions, residence requirements and deadline.

Given the competitiveness of the programme, applicants should allow sufficient time to prepare a strong research or creative proposal that clearly demonstrates both the quality of the proposed project and its relevance to the Global Invisible University.

Important Points Applicants Should Remember

Before applying for an IAS CEU fellowship for 2027/28, prospective candidates should keep several important points in mind:

  • The programme is centred primarily on the social sciences and humanities.
  • Proposed work should connect with at least one of the eight GIU thematic areas.
  • Residential fellowship periods generally range from three to nine months.
  • Artist in Residence fellowships are available for a minimum of three months and up to five months.
  • Non-residential fellowships lasting six to 12 months are available exclusively to eligible Threatened Scholars.
  • Junior and Senior Core Fellows receive a stipend and accommodation.
  • Affiliated Fellows do not receive a stipend from IAS CEU.
  • Housing for Affiliated Fellows is not guaranteed.
  • Applications are assessed through rigorous peer review.
  • Final decisions are made by an independent Selection Committee.
  • Research excellence, applicant track record and thematic relevance are major selection considerations.
  • The programme is highly competitive.
  • Applicants should consult their specific fellowship call for exact application requirements and deadlines.

Conclusion

The IAS CEU Global Invisible University Fellowships 2027/28 provide an important opportunity for scholars, researchers, writers and visual artists seeking dedicated time and an interdisciplinary environment in which to advance ambitious research or creative projects.

Through its different fellowship pathways, the Institute of Advanced Study at Central European University accommodates applicants at different career stages and in different circumstances—from promising junior researchers and established senior academics to creative practitioners, threatened scholars and externally funded researchers.

At the heart of the programme is the Global Invisible University’s ambition to rethink how research, teaching, mentoring and civic engagement can respond to the profound pressures currently affecting higher education and knowledge production worldwide.

Applicants whose work examines democracy, history and memory, inequality, human rights, international institutions, climate justice, media, digital society or changing methods of knowledge production may find particularly strong alignment with the programme’s research priorities.

Because admission is highly competitive, prospective applicants should carefully identify the most appropriate fellowship, study its individual requirements and develop a compelling proposal demonstrating research excellence, a strong track record and clear relevance to the Global Invisible University.

Interested applicants should visit the official IAS CEU fellowship website for the individual 2027/28 calls, detailed eligibility conditions, application procedures and applicable deadlines:

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for the Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027 – Cohort V, a year-long leadership and community development opportunity designed to support emerging Indigenous women leaders who are creating meaningful change within their communities.

Through its Indigenous Women’s Program, Land is Life is inviting Indigenous women from around the world to submit applications for the 2027 fellowship cohort. The program is particularly focused on women who are committed to advancing Indigenous Peoples’ rights, gender equality, land and resource rights, environmental justice, community well-being and sustainable livelihoods.

Successful fellows will receive a comprehensive package of support that combines personalised mentorship, technical assistance, leadership development, international networking opportunities and financial support. Fellows can receive up to USD $3,000 to design and implement a community-level project, in addition to a USD $3,600 stipend to support their participation throughout the fellowship.

Applications opened on 25 August 2026 and must be submitted by 24 September 2026 at 11:00 PM EST.

About the Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027

The Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship is an initiative of Land is Life, a global coalition of Indigenous Peoples working to advance self-determination and collective rights for Indigenous Peoples across the world’s seven sociocultural regions.

Land is Life established its Indigenous Women’s Program in 2022. The program was designed and is led by Indigenous women, with a focus on strengthening the ability of Indigenous women and their organisations to assert their individual and collective rights.

Its work particularly supports Indigenous women in Africa, Asia and throughout the Americas in their efforts to access, use and control land and natural resources, strengthen their livelihoods, and promote and protect the rights of their peoples.

Through the Indigenous Women’s Program, participants have received support including funding, stipends, mentorship and training opportunities. This assistance has also helped Indigenous women leaders participate in international spaces where decisions affecting Indigenous Peoples and their communities are discussed.

The fellowship component began in 2023 and has since supported more than 15 women in successfully implementing community projects.

Purpose of the Indigenous Women’s Fellowship

The year-long fellowship seeks to nurture the next generation of Indigenous women leaders.

Rather than focusing exclusively on theoretical learning, the fellowship supports women who are already taking innovative steps within their communities and gives them the resources, knowledge and networks needed to turn their ideas into practical projects.

The fellowship particularly supports initiatives that contribute to:

  • Gender equality;
  • Recognition and protection of Indigenous Peoples’ land and resource rights;
  • Community well-being;
  • Indigenous women’s leadership;
  • Protection and promotion of Indigenous Peoples’ rights;
  • Stronger community livelihoods;
  • Environmental and climate justice;
  • Indigenous governance and autonomy; and
  • Greater participation of Indigenous women in decision-making.

An important part of the fellowship is the implementation of a community-level project. Applicants are therefore expected to identify an issue affecting their community and propose an achievable initiative that responds to that challenge.

What Does the Land is Life Fellowship Offer?

Selected participants in the 2027 Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship will receive a combination of financial, technical and professional development support.

1. Up to USD $3,000 in Community Project Funding

Each fellow can receive funding and technical support of up to USD $3,000 to design and implement a community-level project.

The project should address issues relevant to Indigenous Peoples and place particular attention on the rights, experiences and needs of Indigenous women and girls.

This component gives fellows the opportunity to translate their leadership ideas into tangible initiatives within their own communities.

2. USD $3,600 Fellowship Stipend

Selected fellows will also receive a USD $3,600 stipend.

The stipend is intended to support each fellow’s participation throughout the program, providing additional financial support as they undertake fellowship activities and work on their community projects.

3. Personalised Mentorship

Participants will receive personalised mentoring from experienced Indigenous women leaders with demonstrated experience in advancing Indigenous Peoples’ rights.

This mentorship gives fellows an opportunity to learn directly from women who have practical leadership, advocacy and community experience.

4. Technical Support

In addition to financial assistance, fellows will receive technical support for the design and implementation of their community projects.

This can help participants develop realistic, achievable projects and strengthen their capacity to manage initiatives that produce meaningful results for their communities.

5. Bimonthly Training and Knowledge Sharing

Fellows will participate in bimonthly training sessions addressing important topics related to Indigenous Peoples’ rights.

These learning opportunities are designed to strengthen participants’ knowledge while encouraging the exchange of ideas, experiences and approaches between Indigenous women from different communities and regions.

6. Leadership Development

Leadership development is a central part of the fellowship.

The program seeks to strengthen the voices of Indigenous women and increase their decision-making power within their communities and beyond.

Participants will have opportunities to develop skills and confidence that can support their continued work as community leaders and advocates.

7. Networking Opportunities

Fellows will be able to build and strengthen relationships with local, regional and global partners and allies.

These networks can be valuable beyond the fellowship itself, particularly for women seeking to expand community initiatives, exchange knowledge or collaborate with other Indigenous leaders and organisations.

8. Advocacy Support

The fellowship also provides advocacy support that can help participants engage in national and international decision-making spaces.

This creates opportunities for Indigenous women leaders to contribute their perspectives and community experiences to wider discussions concerning Indigenous rights and related issues.

Six Central Themes of the Indigenous Women’s Program

Applicants must develop a community project aligned with the central themes identified by the Indigenous Women’s Program.

The six areas are:

1. Climate Change and Environmental Justice

Projects can address issues such as:

  • Climate change adaptation and mitigation;
  • Biodiversity protection; and
  • Critical examination of false climate solutions.

Indigenous communities are often directly connected to their territories and natural resources, making Indigenous leadership particularly important in discussions about environmental protection and climate resilience.

2. Land Rights and Territorial Defence

Projects may focus on protecting Indigenous territories from threats such as:

  • Extractive activities;
  • Forced evictions;
  • Illegal logging;
  • Illegal mining; and
  • Other pressures affecting Indigenous territories.

This theme also encompasses Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) protocols.

3. Food Sovereignty and Livelihoods

Potential initiatives can address:

  • Agroecology;
  • Seed sovereignty; and
  • Economic alternatives to industrial agribusiness.

Projects under this theme can explore ways Indigenous communities can strengthen control over their food systems while protecting traditional practices and developing sustainable livelihoods.

4. Health and Well-Being

Projects can address a range of community health and well-being priorities, including:

  • Access to traditional medicine;
  • Mental health support following disasters;
  • Maternal health;
  • Child health; and
  • Violence prevention.

5. Economic Empowerment and Livelihood Strengthening

This theme can include projects related to:

  • Community enterprises;
  • Market access;
  • Sustainable income generation; and
  • Women’s economic leadership.

The focus is on strengthening economic opportunities in ways that support Indigenous communities and women’s leadership.

6. Governance

Projects can also support Indigenous organisations and communities in strengthening governance.

Areas may include:

  • Strengthening organisational structures;
  • Supporting autonomy models; and
  • Promoting approaches rooted in traditional governance systems.

Who Can Apply for the Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027?

Applicants must meet several eligibility requirements.

Age Requirement

Applicants must be Indigenous women between 18 and 35 years old.

Educational Background

Land is Life states that priority will be given to Indigenous women who do not hold a master’s or doctoral degree.

This is intended to expand access to advanced learning and leadership development opportunities.

Importantly, the source does not state that applicants must possess a particular undergraduate degree. Instead, it specifically identifies the absence of a master’s or doctoral degree as a priority consideration.

Language Requirement

Applicants must be able to speak fluently in at least one of the following languages:

  • English;
  • French; or
  • Spanish.

Previous Fellowship Participation

Applicants must not have previously been a Land is Life fellow.

Former fellows are therefore not eligible to participate again under this requirement.

Geographic Considerations

The call is open to Indigenous women from all seven sociocultural regions.

However, Land is Life states that priority will be given to applicants from countries that have not previously been represented in the Indigenous Women’s Fellowship Program.

Countries that have already been represented include:

  • Indonesia;
  • Tanzania;
  • Panama;
  • Ecuador;
  • Peru;
  • Colombia;
  • Kenya;
  • Mali;
  • Philippines;
  • Democratic Republic of Congo;
  • Nepal;
  • Mexico; and
  • Bolivia.

Being from one of these countries is not explicitly listed as an automatic disqualification. Rather, the announcement states that priority will be given to applicants from countries that have not previously participated.

What Will Selected Fellows Be Expected to Do?

Successful applicants will take on several responsibilities during the fellowship.

1. Design and Implement a Community Project

Each fellow must design and implement a community-level project.

The project must be completed within 10 months.

This is a major component of the fellowship and applicants should therefore develop a proposal that is realistic, relevant to their community and achievable within the available timeframe and resources.

2. Advance Indigenous Peoples’ Rights

Fellows are expected to support their communities in advancing the promotion and protection of Indigenous Peoples’ rights.

Particular attention should be given to the rights of Indigenous women and girls.

3. Participate in Fellowship Activities

Fellows must actively participate in:

  • Bimonthly virtual training sessions; and
  • Peer-learning activities.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to commit time not only to their community projects but also to the learning and collaborative components of the fellowship.

How to Apply for the Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Fellowship 2027

Eligible applicants should complete the following application process.

Step 1: Complete the Online Application Form

Applicants must complete the official application form provided by Land is Life.

The application form can be accessed through the official fellowship announcement and application portal.

Step 2: Develop a Community Project Proposal

Applicants need to develop a proposed community project that promotes Indigenous Peoples’ rights, with particular attention to Indigenous women and girls.

The proposed project should align with at least one of the central themes of the Indigenous Women’s Program.

Applicants should therefore consider how their project relates to areas such as climate and environmental justice, land and territorial rights, food sovereignty, health and well-being, economic empowerment or Indigenous governance.

The original call specifically asks for proposals with clear and achievable goals and a strong commitment to Indigenous Peoples’ rights, gender equality and community well-being.

Step 3: Obtain a Letter of Recommendation

Applicants must provide a letter of recommendation from an appropriate Indigenous source.

The recommendation can come from:

  • An Indigenous Peoples organisation;
  • A representative or leader from the applicant’s territory; or
  • An equivalent official source.

Applicants should allow sufficient time to obtain this letter before the application deadline.

Application Option for Applicants With Limited Internet Access

Land is Life has provided an alternative process for Indigenous women who have little or no reliable internet access.

Applicants experiencing difficulties completing the online form should contact:

info@landislife.org

In the email, applicants should explain that they are experiencing difficulty completing the application form and request that the application questions be sent to them by email.

After receiving the questions, applicants can prepare their responses and return them by email.

However, the same application deadline applies. Land is Life clearly states that applications must be received before the deadline and that late or incomplete applications will not be considered.

Important Dates for the 2027 Fellowship

Applicants should take note of the following timeline:

  • Applications open: 25 August 2026
  • Application deadline: 24 September 2026 at 11:00 PM EST
  • Application assessment: 30 September to 29 October 2026
  • Results announced: 9 November 2026 via email
  • Fellowship starting date: 12 January 2027

Applicants are strongly encouraged to prepare and submit their materials well ahead of the closing date rather than waiting until the final hours.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027 – Cohort V is 24 September 2026 at 11:00 PM EST.

Applications submitted after the deadline or applications that are incomplete will not be considered.

Applicants should also pay close attention to the stated EST time zone, particularly when applying from Africa, Asia, the Pacific, Europe or other regions where the local closing time may fall on a different date or time.

APPLY NOW

Why This Fellowship Is an Important Opportunity for Emerging Indigenous Women Leaders

The Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship is distinctive because it combines leadership development with practical community action.

Successful applicants are not simply participating in training sessions. They will have an opportunity to design and implement their own community projects while receiving financial resources, technical support and mentorship from experienced Indigenous women leaders.

The combination of up to USD $3,000 in project funding and a USD $3,600 fellowship stipend can provide emerging leaders with resources to develop initiatives responding directly to priorities identified within their communities.

At the same time, bimonthly training, mentorship, peer learning, networking and advocacy support can help participants build capabilities and relationships that extend beyond their individual projects.

For Indigenous women who are already working to protect territories, strengthen livelihoods, advance gender equality, preserve Indigenous rights or improve community well-being, the fellowship provides an opportunity to develop those efforts within a structured international program.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

While Land is Life does not provide a scoring formula in the announcement, applicants should closely follow the requirements of the open call.

A strong proposal should clearly explain:

  1. The community challenge: What specific issue does the project seek to address?
  2. Why the issue matters: How does the problem affect Indigenous Peoples, particularly Indigenous women and girls?
  3. The proposed solution: What activities will the applicant undertake?
  4. The objectives: What clear and achievable goals will the project pursue?
  5. Community relevance: How will the initiative benefit or support the applicant’s community?
  6. Program alignment: Which of the Indigenous Women’s Program’s central themes does the project address?
  7. Feasibility: Can the project realistically be completed within the required 10-month period?
  8. Rights-based impact: How will the project contribute to Indigenous Peoples’ rights, gender equality or community well-being?

Applicants should ensure that every required component, including the recommendation letter, is prepared before submitting the application.

Conclusion

The Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027 – Cohort V offers an important opportunity for emerging Indigenous women leaders to strengthen their leadership abilities while implementing practical projects in their own communities.

With personalised mentorship, bimonthly training, technical assistance, networking and advocacy opportunities, up to USD $3,000 in community project funding and a USD $3,600 participation stipend, the fellowship provides both financial and capacity-building support.

The program is particularly relevant for Indigenous women working on issues connected to climate and environmental justice, territorial and land rights, food sovereignty, health and well-being, economic empowerment, sustainable livelihoods and Indigenous governance.

Eligible Indigenous women between the ages of 18 and 35 who can communicate fluently in English, French or Spanish and have not previously participated as a Land is Life fellow are encouraged to review the requirements carefully and prepare their community project proposals.

Applications close on 24 September 2026 at 11:00 PM EST. Interested applicants should complete their applications, project proposals and recommendation letters before the deadline to ensure their submissions are considered.

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
Applications will open on 1 October 2026 for the Maastricht University Social Justice Scholarship 2027–2028, a highly competitive full scholarship for talented international students who want to pursue the full-time Master’s programme in Globalisation and Law at Maastricht University in the Netherlands.

The scholarship is particularly aimed at applicants who have already demonstrated a meaningful commitment to human rights and/or strengthening the rule of law through academic, extracurricular, professional or community initiatives.

Only one full scholarship is awarded each academic year, making this an exceptionally selective funding opportunity.

The scholarship provides substantial financial support for the entire 13-month programme, including:

  • Full tuition fees
  • €20,150 in living expenses for 13 months
  • Health and liability insurance
  • Visa application costs
  • Mandatory pre-academic training
  • Participation costs for the first block of the International Student Ambassador Programme
  • Arranged accommodation as part of the scholarship package

The scholarship is available to applicants from outside the European Union and European Economic Area, subject to additional nationality, residence, academic and visa requirements. Maastricht University describes the programme as supporting its commitments to diversity, inclusivity and strengthening the rule of law, including through its wider human rights and peace initiatives.

There are two particularly important deadlines:

Master’s programme application deadline: 10 December 2026

Scholarship application deadline: 1 February 2027

Applicants should understand that they must first apply to the Globalisation and Law Master’s programme before completing the separate Social Justice Scholarship application.

About the Maastricht University Social Justice Scholarship

The UM Social Justice Scholarship is an international funding programme created by Maastricht University to support academically excellent students who have demonstrated a record of contributing to:

  • Human rights
  • Rule of law
  • Social justice
  • Related initiatives and projects

The scholarship reflects Maastricht University’s broader emphasis on diversity, inclusion and global engagement.

The University explicitly connects the scholarship to its Global Engagement Policy and to its commitment to strengthening the rule of law.

Unlike a general international scholarship available across all Maastricht University programmes, this scholarship is tied to one specific Master’s degree:

Globalisation and Law

Applicants seeking admission to another Maastricht University Master’s programme cannot use that programme to qualify for this particular scholarship.

Number of Scholarships Available

Maastricht University awards:

One full Social Justice Scholarship per academic year.

This means competition is likely to be extremely strong.

Academic excellence alone is therefore unlikely to be sufficient.

Applicants must also demonstrate a convincing combination of:

  • Strong academic results
  • Clear motivation
  • Previous human rights and/or rule-of-law engagement
  • Financial need
  • Strong recommendation
  • Programme fit
  • Potential for future impact

The scholarship is designed for highly talented students from outside the EU/EEA who have already made demonstrable contributions to human rights or the rule of law.

Eligible Master’s Programme

The scholarship is available only for the:

Full-time Master’s programme Globalisation and Law

at Maastricht University.

Applicants must apply for the:

2027–2028 academic year.

Applications to other Law Faculty programmes do not qualify for the UM Social Justice Scholarship.

This restriction is explicitly stated in the application procedure.

Why Globalisation and Law?

The programme is particularly relevant for students interested in legal questions shaped by international and transnational developments.

The scholarship’s own selection criteria emphasize applicants with previous involvement in:

  • Human rights
  • Rule of law
  • Social justice-related activities

As a result, it may be especially attractive to applicants whose academic or professional interests concern:

  • International law
  • Human rights law
  • Global governance
  • Rule of law
  • Legal institutions
  • International justice
  • Legal responses to globalization
  • Rights protection

Applicants should still review the actual Globalisation and Law curriculum before applying and ensure that their interests align with the programme itself.

Scholarship Duration

The UM Social Justice Scholarship covers:

13 months

for the one-year Globalisation and Law Master’s programme.

This extended funding period is important because the scholarship is designed to support students not only with tuition but also with living expenses throughout their stay.

Scholarship Financial Benefits

The Social Justice Scholarship is a substantial full funding package.

For the 2027–2028 cycle, the published support includes several components.

Living Expenses: €20,150

Scholarship recipients receive:

€20,150 for 13 months

in living expenses.

This is equivalent to:

€1,550 per month.

The living allowance is paid to the student by the Maastricht University International Services Desk.

The published amount is subject to change for the 2027–2028 academic year.

Monthly Living Expense Breakdown

Maastricht University provides a detailed estimate showing how the monthly €1,550 living allowance is intended to cover expenses.

The indicative monthly breakdown is:

  • Housing: €960
  • Groceries and personal hygiene: €160
  • Telephone: €60
  • Travel: €100
  • Books and study materials: €90
  • Clothing, hobbies and going out: €125
  • Miscellaneous: €55

These amounts are estimates and may change.

Applicants should therefore understand that the €20,150 living allowance is designed to cover normal student living costs rather than being an additional discretionary cash award on top of accommodation and everyday expenses.

Tuition Fees

The scholarship covers:

Tuition fees at cost.

The Maastricht University International Services Desk arranges and pays the tuition component.

For scholarship recipients, this effectively provides full tuition funding for the eligible programme.

Health and Liability Insurance

The scholarship includes:

€700 for health and liability insurance

based on the current published amount.

The International Services Desk arranges and pays for the insurance.

The amount may change for 2027–2028.

Visa Application Costs

The scholarship also covers:

Visa application costs at cost.

These are arranged and paid by the University’s International Services Desk.

This is particularly important because the scholarship is specifically intended for many students who will need Dutch immigration authorization.

Applicants must nevertheless meet all eligibility conditions for obtaining the appropriate entry visa and residence permit.

Pre-Academic Training Costs

The scholarship covers the cost of Maastricht University’s:

Pre-Academic Training programme

at cost.

This training is not optional for scholarship recipients.

It is a:

Mandatory two-week component

and is scheduled to begin in the:

First week of August 2027.

Successful applicants should therefore plan to arrive in time to participate.

International Student Ambassador Programme

The scholarship also covers the cost of the:

International Student Ambassador Programme, or ISAP

for the:

First block only.

Applicants should consult Maastricht University for the current structure of this programme and any later participation costs that may fall outside the scholarship.

Accommodation Is Mandatory

A particularly important condition of the Social Justice Scholarship is its accommodation arrangement.

Scholarship recipients are allocated a room until:

July 2028

and accepting the scholarship means accepting this accommodation.

The University explicitly states that:

Refusing the allocated room results in cancellation of the scholarship.

This is therefore not an optional housing service.

It is a mandatory part of the scholarship package.

Accommodation and Families

The accommodation allocated to scholarship students is:

Not suitable for partners, spouses and/or children.

Applicants planning to move to the Netherlands with family members should consider this condition carefully.

Maastricht University does state that accommodation preferences connected to considerations such as religious beliefs will be taken into account where possible.

Is Airfare Included?

No.

The scholarship explicitly states that:

Air tickets are not included.

Students are responsible for paying for their own flight or other travel to the Netherlands.

This is an important distinction when describing the scholarship as “fully funded.”

It comprehensively covers tuition, living support, accommodation allocation, insurance, visa costs and training, but it does not cover airfare.

Cleaning Fee

The scholarship also does not cover the accommodation cleaning fee.

The current estimate is approximately:

€75

and must be paid directly to Maastricht Housing by the student.

Who Can Apply?

Applicants must satisfy all published eligibility conditions.

This includes requirements concerning:

  • Nationality
  • Residence status
  • Academic programme
  • Human rights/rule-of-law involvement
  • Academic performance
  • Age
  • Visa eligibility
  • Previous Master’s education

Nationality Requirement

Applicants must hold nationality in a country:

Outside the EU/EEA, Switzerland and Surinam.

They must also meet the requirements for obtaining the appropriate Dutch:

  • Entry visa
  • Residence permit

This means the scholarship is specifically aimed at international students from outside those listed jurisdictions.

Dual Nationality Restriction

Applicants are not eligible if they have dual nationality from:

  • An EU/EEA country, or
  • Switzerland

A candidate holding both a non-EU nationality and an EU nationality would therefore not satisfy this condition.

Existing Schengen Residence Permit

Applicants who already hold a residence permit for another Schengen country may still potentially apply, but special conditions apply.

The permit must remain valid until at least:

2 September 2027

If it expires before that date, applicants can only apply for the scholarship through the applicable MVV visa procedure from their home country.

Applicants with complicated immigration status should review Maastricht University’s Visa Office guidance before applying.

Programme Admission Requirement

Applicants must have applied for:

Full-time Globalisation and Law

at Maastricht University for:

2027–2028

and must submit the complete programme application, meeting all admission requirements, before:

10 December 2026.

This deadline is earlier than the scholarship deadline.

Applicants cannot wait until February to start their Master’s application.

Human Rights or Rule-of-Law Contribution

One of the defining requirements is that applicants must have already made a:

Proven contribution to supporting the rule of law and/or human rights

through:

  • Intracurricular initiatives
  • Extracurricular initiatives
  • Projects

This means simply stating an interest in human rights is unlikely to satisfy the requirement.

Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate actual involvement.

What Could Count as Human Rights or Rule-of-Law Experience?

The official source does not provide an exhaustive list, but applicants should use their application to document relevant activities clearly.

Potential evidence could include, where genuinely applicable:

  • Human rights advocacy
  • Legal aid
  • Student human rights initiatives
  • Rule-of-law programmes
  • NGO work
  • Community projects
  • Research
  • Relevant internships
  • Policy initiatives
  • Legal awareness programmes

The strongest applications will describe both:

  • What the applicant did
  • What contribution or impact resulted

rather than listing organization names without context.

GPA Requirement

Applicants must demonstrate excellent academic results.

The minimum required GPA is:

7.5 out of 10

or equivalent.

The application guidance further explains that this corresponds to approximately:

  • 75% out of 100%, or
  • 3.0 out of 4.0

depending on the grading system.

Applicants must provide both:

  1. An official transcript or university document showing their GPA.
  2. A document explaining their institution’s grading system.

GPA Must Be Cumulative

The scholarship application instructions state that Maastricht University only accepts candidates with a:

Cumulative GPA of at least 75% of the maximum scale in the Bachelor’s degree.

Applicants should therefore not rely only on a particularly strong final semester if their cumulative result does not meet the threshold.

Age Limit

Applicants must be:

35 years old or younger on 1 September 2027.

Candidates older than 35 on that date are not eligible under the published rules.

Previous Master’s Degree

Applicants who already hold a Master’s degree are not automatically excluded.

However:

Preference will be given to candidates who have not yet obtained a Master’s degree.

This distinction matters.

An applicant with a previous Master’s may still apply if all other conditions are met, but they may be at a disadvantage compared with an otherwise similarly strong candidate seeking their first Master’s.

Only One Scholarship Application

Candidates may:

Apply once and for one scholarship only.

After submission, Maastricht University will not add or replace documents.

Applicants should therefore check every document carefully before submitting the final scholarship application.

Important Application Dates

Applications for the Social Justice Scholarship open on:

1 October 2026.

The major deadlines are:

Globalisation and Law programme application

10 December 2026

UM Social Justice Scholarship application

1 February 2027

By the scholarship deadline, candidates must have completed the relevant registration requirements except for:

  • Legal residence
  • Tuition payment
  • Hard copy of the diploma

Application Process

The Social Justice Scholarship application involves two main stages.

Step 1: Apply for Globalisation and Law

Applicants must first apply to the:

Globalisation and Law Master’s programme

through:

Studielink

After submitting the programme application, the applicant will receive a Maastricht University student ID number.

This student number is required for the scholarship application.

Programme Application Deadline

For scholarship eligibility, the complete Globalisation and Law application must be submitted by:

10 December 2026.

This includes fulfilling the admission requirements.

Applicants should not confuse this with any later general programme deadline that may apply to candidates who are not seeking the Social Justice Scholarship.

APPLY HERE

Handling Fees

If the programme requires an admissions handling fee:

The scholarship does not cover it.

The applicant is personally responsible for paying any applicable fee by:

10 December 2026.

Step 2: Complete the Scholarship Application Form

After obtaining a Maastricht University account and student number, applicants complete the scholarship application through the official online form.

The University accepts scholarship applications only through this form.

Supporting documents may be uploaded in:

  • DOC
  • DOCX
  • PDF

Please fill out the application form here.

Required Scholarship Documents

Candidates must prepare several important documents.

1. Curriculum Vitae

The CV must:

  • Be current
  • Include relevant educational information
  • Include relevant employment experience
  • Mention awards and prizes where applicable
  • Be no longer than two A4 pages

Because the scholarship is highly competitive, applicants should prioritize evidence relevant to:

  • Academic excellence
  • Human rights
  • Rule of law
  • Leadership
  • Community involvement
  • Professional development

2. Motivation Letter

Applicants must use the:

Official Maastricht University scholarship motivation letter template.

The template focuses specifically on motivation for the scholarship.

Applicants are instructed to emphasize:

What they have already done to improve human rights.

This is especially important.

The scholarship is not intended solely for applicants who want to work in human rights in the future.

It seeks people with a proven record of engagement already.

How to Strengthen the Motivation Letter

A competitive motivation letter should explain:

  • Why Globalisation and Law fits the applicant’s goals
  • What human rights/rule-of-law work the applicant has already undertaken
  • What role the applicant personally played
  • What impact resulted
  • Why the scholarship is necessary
  • How Maastricht University will help the applicant extend that work

Applicants should avoid making the letter entirely aspirational.

Evidence of past contribution is a formal eligibility factor.

3. Proof of Academic Excellence

Candidates must upload:

  1. Transcript or official university documentation showing a GPA of at least 7.5/10 or equivalent.
  2. Documentation explaining the grading scale.

This requirement is particularly important for applicants whose universities use grading systems that differ substantially from the Dutch system.

4. Personal Statement of Financial Need

Applicants must submit a:

Personal statement of financial needs.

The University asks candidates to explain why receiving the scholarship would benefit them.

Examples of relevant personal circumstances explicitly mentioned include:

  • Financial difficulty
  • Sole-parent responsibilities
  • Caretaking responsibilities
  • Medical conditions
  • Disability
  • Refugee status

The statement should be factual and personal rather than generic.

5. Reference Letter

Applicants must submit:

One reference letter.

The University provides specific scholarship reference-letter guidelines that should be sent to the referee.

Eligible referees include:

  • Current or former professors
  • Lecturers
  • Employers

Family members cannot act as referees.

Reference Letter Date Requirement

Recommendation letters must be:

Dated no earlier than February 2026.

Letters failing to follow the official guidelines will not be considered, which can cause an application to be treated as incomplete.

Applicants Upload the Reference Letter Themselves

Unlike some scholarship systems where referees upload recommendations directly, the UM Social Justice Scholarship requires:

The applicant to upload the reference letter.

The referee cannot submit it directly through the scholarship application.

Applicants should therefore request their reference well before the deadline.

6. Referee Contact Details

Applicants must also provide one referee’s contact information.

This includes:

  • Relationship to the applicant
  • Work telephone number with country code
  • Work or institutional email address

A recommendation linked only to a:

Personal email address

will be rejected.

The University may contact the referee to verify the authenticity of the recommendation.

Selection Process

Because only one scholarship is available, selection involves several stages.

Stage 1: Completeness Check

After:

1 February 2027

the UM International Services Desk checks whether applications are complete.

Incomplete applications do not progress.

Stage 2: Faculty Review

Complete applications are sent to the:

UM Law Faculty

in:

February 2027.

Faculty reviewers assess eligible candidates.

Stage 3: Top Three Candidates

The Law Faculty selects and ranks its:

Top three scholarship applicants

and sends their files to the International Services Desk for a final check in:

March 2027.

This means only a very small final group moves forward to the interview stage.

Stage 4: Online Interview

By the end of March, Maastricht University confirms the Faculty selections and invites selected candidates to:

An online interview.

Candidates invited to interview must prepare an:

Action plan

explaining how studying at Maastricht University will enable them to contribute to strengthening:

  • Human rights
  • Rule of law

in their home country and/or elsewhere.

This makes future impact an explicit part of final selection.

Preparing the Action Plan

Applicants who reach the interview should be prepared to explain:

  • The human rights or rule-of-law problem they want to address
  • What skills or knowledge they currently lack
  • How Globalisation and Law will help fill that gap
  • What they plan to do after graduation
  • Which institutions, communities or systems they want to influence
  • How they will translate the Master’s degree into practical impact

A generic career plan will likely be less persuasive than a specific and realistic pathway.

Final Results

Following interviews, applicants will be informed of their status in:

April 2027

with final statuses communicated by:

The beginning of May 2027 at the latest.

Possible outcomes include:

  • Selected
  • Waitlisted
  • Rejected

Waitlisted candidates will receive a final selected/rejected result during May 2027.

Accepting the Scholarship

Successful candidates must:

Sign and return the scholarship award letter

to the UM International Services Desk.

This formally confirms acceptance of the scholarship and its associated conditions, including the mandatory accommodation requirement.

Pre-Academic Training

Scholarship recipients must participate in the:

Two-week UM Pre-Academic Training programme

beginning in:

The first week of August 2027.

Successful candidates should therefore plan their immigration and arrival arrangements accordingly.

What the Scholarship Does Not Cover

Despite its comprehensive funding package, several costs remain the responsibility of the applicant.

The scholarship does not cover:

  • Air tickets
  • Approximately €75 accommodation cleaning fee
  • Programme handling fees where applicable

Applicants should budget for these expenses in advance.

Important Dates at a Glance

Scholarship applications open: 1 October 2026

Globalisation and Law application deadline for scholarship candidates: 10 December 2026

Scholarship application deadline: 1 February 2027

Completeness checks: After 1 February 2027

Law Faculty review: February 2027

Top three ranking: March 2027

Interviews: Around late March/April 2027

Final decisions: April to early May 2027

Mandatory Pre-Academic Training: First week of August 2027

Academic year: 2027–2028

Scholarship Benefits at a Glance

Number of awards: 1

Programme: Globalisation and Law

Duration: 13 months

Living allowance: €20,150

Monthly equivalent: €1,550

Tuition fees: Covered

Health and liability insurance: €700, arranged and paid

Visa application costs: Covered at cost

Pre-Academic Training: Covered

International Student Ambassador Programme: First block covered

Accommodation: Mandatory room allocated as part of scholarship arrangements

Airfare: Not covered

Cleaning fee: Not covered

Eligibility Checklist

Before applying, candidates should confirm that they:

  1. Hold nationality outside the EU/EEA, Switzerland and Surinam.
  2. Do not hold dual EU/EEA or Swiss nationality.
  3. Can meet Dutch visa and residence requirements.
  4. Have applied to full-time Globalisation and Law for 2027–2028.
  5. Complete their Master’s application by 10 December 2026.
  6. Meet all Globalisation and Law admission requirements.
  7. Have demonstrated previous support for human rights and/or the rule of law.
  8. Are no older than 35 on 1 September 2027.
  9. Have a GPA of at least 7.5/10 or equivalent.
  10. Can provide documentation explaining their grading scale.
  11. Understand that applicants without a previous Master’s receive preference.
  12. Submit only one scholarship application.
  13. Have all documents ready before submitting because they cannot be replaced afterward.
  14. Are prepared to accept the mandatory scholarship accommodation.
  15. Can participate in the mandatory August 2027 Pre-Academic Training.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Demonstrate Proven Human Rights Impact

This is one of the most important features of the scholarship.

Do not simply write:

“I am passionate about human rights.”

Instead, explain:

  • What you did
  • Why you became involved
  • Your personal responsibilities
  • Who benefited
  • What changed
  • What you learned

The scholarship explicitly requires previous contribution.

2. Make Your Motivation Letter Evidence-Based

Connect your past activities with your future goals.

A strong narrative might follow:

Past contribution → current knowledge gap → Maastricht training → future human rights/rule-of-law impact

This creates a clear argument for why the scholarship should be invested in you.

3. Explain Why Globalisation and Law Specifically

Avoid describing Maastricht University only in broad terms.

Research the actual programme and identify:

  • Courses
  • Faculty expertise
  • Legal themes
  • Research opportunities

that directly support your intended work.

4. Treat Financial Need as a Serious Application Component

The personal financial statement is not simply an administrative formality.

Explain your financial circumstances honestly and specifically.

Where relevant, describe issues such as:

  • Family responsibilities
  • Refugee background
  • Financial constraints
  • Disability
  • Caregiving

without exaggeration.

5. Select a Strong Referee

Your referee should be someone who can credibly discuss:

  • Academic ability
  • Professional qualities
  • Human rights involvement
  • Rule-of-law work
  • Potential for impact

The referee must use a professional or institutional email.

6. Prepare for the Interview Early

Because shortlisted candidates need to present an action plan, start considering:

What will you do with this degree?

before submitting the scholarship application.

The strongest candidates will likely demonstrate a realistic pathway from education to practical impact.

Conclusion

The Maastricht University Social Justice Scholarship 2027–2028 is an exceptional full funding opportunity for highly talented international students who want to pursue the Master’s in Globalisation and Law while building on an existing record of engagement with human rights and the rule of law.

Only one scholarship is awarded annually, making the programme highly competitive.

The financial package includes €20,150 in living support for 13 months, full tuition funding, health and liability insurance, visa application costs, mandatory pre-academic training and other programme-related support. Maastricht University also allocates accommodation to scholarship recipients as a mandatory part of the award.

Applicants must come from outside the EU/EEA, Switzerland and Surinam, may not hold dual EU/EEA or Swiss nationality, must be no older than 35 on 1 September 2027 and must have a minimum GPA equivalent to 7.5/10 or 75% of the maximum scale. They must also demonstrate a proven contribution to human rights and/or the rule of law.

Candidates seeking the scholarship must complete their application to the Globalisation and Law programme by 10 December 2026, while the final Social Justice Scholarship deadline is 1 February 2027.

Selection involves an initial completeness check, Law Faculty assessment, ranking of the top three candidates and an online interview requiring an action plan explaining how the Maastricht degree will help the applicant strengthen human rights or the rule of law in their country or elsewhere.

For applicants with excellent academic results, demonstrated social-justice engagement and a clear vision for translating legal education into practical impact, the UM Social Justice Scholarship represents a rare opportunity to complete a fully funded Master’s degree in the Netherlands.
